Mr. Speaker, I have a particular interest in this Bill, partly because of the importance of Air Canada to my community of Winnipeg, but also because my own experience when I was Minister of Transport brought me into a close examination of some of these issues and questions. In fact, there was a suggestion, when the announcement was first made by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), that the Conservative Government was basing its policies on my initial objectives and goals. As I pointed out at the time, I only wish it had. I think we would have had a much better Bill and a much better presentation of the role of Air Canada if it had continued to follow the pattern and development of airline policy that we started back in 1983-84.
I would like to spend the time I have this afternoon by outlining the steps that were taken and why I think this is not the right Bill. It does not suit the purpose of proper airline development in Canada. In the summer of 1983 when I took over the Transport portfolio, virtually all major Canadian airlines were in deep financial trouble. Two of the private firms were close to bankruptcy. Air Canada had very large losses and was losing a substantial number of customers on its existing airlines. It required an immediate response.
We immediately established a series of working groups to examine what changes could be made in airline policy that would restore to the airline industry the predominant role it has always played. We kept in mind that the airline industry has a special role in Canada because of our geography, our climate and because of our dependence on trade and commerce. The exchange of people and goods by air has always been one of the important factors in allowing us to build and grow and developmemt.
That was recognized by previous Governments back in the 1930s and 1940s when they had to establish a public airline because private airlines were not prepared to undertake that task. By the time we reached the 1980s, conditions had changed radically and altered the role of the public airline. After a very exhaustive and internal examination by a number of Departments, and an examination of the American experience with deregulation, it was my judgment that one way we could stimulate further development in airline activity would be to loosen the rules. So we announced in the spring of 1984 a new airline policy that substantially changed the rules applied by the Canadian Transport Commission. We gave the airlines far greater freedom to set prices, to choose routes and to engage in a number of other initiatives that would allow them to attract customers. The frequent flyer program was a direct result of those changes in rules and regulations in the spring of 1984.
At the same time it was clear to me that if we were going to move to loosen or liberalize the airline regulatory system, we also had to look at the role of the public airline in that context. If we were to follow the American pattern of full and total deregulation, it would obviously put Air Canada into a very awkward position, together with the private airlines. It is very

June 3, 1988
Air Canada
difficult in a totally deregulated environment to have a public airline and private airlines competing. However, it was not my feeling that we should necessarily move toward the full deregulation because in examining the American experience, it was clear there was a number of serious problems related to that American experience. One problem was the whole question of labour relations. One of the by-products of deregulation was a severe and abusive treatment of workers. People were laid off. They lost their jobs and their livelihood without any due compensation or retraining or any opportunity to ensure that their workers' rights would be honoured or protected.
Second, there were some real concerns about safety. There is no question that by having full and open entry we were going to give an invitation to a number of airlines to come into the business without due regard for the proper accountability or safety that was required. Third, and this is a little known fact, under deregulation, the Americans had a very expensive program by which they promoted the development of smaller airlines connecting regional points. They would be prepared to subsidize in a substantial manner airlines that would provide connections to smaller regional areas in Alaska or parts of their continental expanse. That was seen by the Americans as a corollary of any deregulation atmosphere. It was a pure deregulation, in other words. There were also, I think, very severe question marks about the concentration of the airline industry.
At the same time as announcing the airline policy in April of 1984, we put forward a clear term of reference to the Transport Committee of the House of Commons to examine those kinds of questions. First, should we proceed with further liberalizing of the airline regulations? And what should be the role of Air Canada in that particular environment? Specifically that term of reference included an examination of safety, labour relations, merger and anti-competition policy, supply of services to out of place regions. We said that before any further changes would be instituted, the House of Commons Transport Committee, in keeping with the spirit of having a Commons committee engaged in policy making, should undertake a series of extensive hearings across Canada and undertake the proper research and examination and come forward with its recommendations.
Unfortunately, the election in 1984 brought that term of reference to an end. The then Minister of Transport, the present Deputy Prime Minister, cancelled that term of reference. Therefore, there has never been an opportunity in this country for Canadians to express themselves in an open and public way on these very large and serious questions related to airline deregulation and to the role of Air Canada. For the life of me, I do not understand why the new Government, when it came into power in 1984, refused to continue with what should have been an open and serious examination and inquiry into those very important questions. Instead, it retreated back into the bureaucracy, I suppose, and came up
with plans for deregulation and the role of Air Canada without any form of public reference or public examination.
Therefore, those questions went unexamined and to this day are still unexamined. They have not been looked at, nor have Canadians had an opportunity to make themselves heard.
In addition, it was also my feeling that the Government of Canada, as the sole shareholder of Air Canada, had the responsibility to begin examining airline policy and Air Canada not simply in purely transportation terms, but also in large economic development terms. As a renewed and intense competition internationally, we were looking at the development of new technologies, particularly in the aerospace industry. We were certainly looking at increasing the concentration of technology in the central part of Canada, not broadly shared by other parts of Canada. One of the reference I began to examine as Minister of Transport was the question of whether the public role of Air Canada should also include its responsibility to carry with it economic development benefits. That substantially broadened the kind of framework of analysis and accounting that should be applied to that very important Crown agency.
I do not know what happened to that examination. The people of Canada spoke their wisdom in September of 1984 and I was no longer a Transport Minister, so I do not know what happened to that particular internal study we had begun to determine how Air Canada itself could become a major instrument of public policy in terms of economic development.
I would suggest that the concerns we had in 1983-84 about that role were certainly exacerbated and enhanced as we saw what began to happen. The CF-18 decision was a clear example of how the aerospace industry, which could provide a major sharing of technological benefits across Canada, was in fact denied. Instead, the legitimate case for Winnipeg, proven beyond a doubt in terms of economic and financial criteria, was rejected. It was decided for political reasons to place it in the City of Montreal.
Similarly, the situation with Airbus is another question mark. As Air Canada now decides to replace its 727 fleet with a brand new generation of aircraft, the key questions are: "Where will the subcontracting for that Airbus be made and where will the maintenance be carried out?" Those public decisions have a great deal to do with regional development in Canada. If we simply allow the market forces to play, then what we will see happening, once more, is a concentration of that technology, of that new sort of advanced frontier level work concentrated in a very small region of Canada.
The history of Canada has been that we have not relied upon market forces to build it, but that our forefathers, and Sir John A. Macdonald at the time of Confederation, said that if it were simply up to the market, there would not be a Canada. He said that there would be a north-south economic integration with the United States. In order to have an east-west economic
June 3, 1988

union there had to be a form of public intervention. In Sir John A's day it was the railroad that did it. In our generation it may be the computer, or information systems, or the aerospace industry that does it. Nevertheless there has to be a public decision to ensure that those economic benefits are broadly and widely shared so that all of Canada becomes part of that system of new economic activity.
We come to the point as to whether those kinds of considerations were in fact brought to bear in both the deregulation initiative and the Air Canada Bill. The answer is clearly no. Nowhere in any of the speeches by the Ministers introducing these measures was there any consideration of those factors or criteria-none whatsoever. It is simply an attempt, as they say, to find ways of refinancing Air Canada, and then letting the competitive market-place take its course.
The reason I oppose the Bill is for that reason primarily. I still believe that there is a public purpose for Air Canada. There is still a very important set of public policies that can be carried out by a national airline.
This legislation, as hybrid as it may be, and as much as it attempts to say that we are going to protect the maintenance base in Winnipeg, does not say that that maintenance base will continue to provide work on the frontier of the aerospace industry. It is just as easy for that maintenance base to do maintenance work on junk aircraft, DC-3s or older jet aircraft, which will put it in the back lot of technological development.
The only way that a fair share of technology can be assured is through public policy. But if the primary carrier in the airline industry of that public policy is being taken away, then no longer can any type of judgment or guidance as to how it should be carried out be given. Similarly, it is very clear from the way that this has been handled that the Government has given no account to those concerns that were raised and should have been examined by the Transport Committee in 1984. There are still very serious safety questions related to the deregulation of our airlines.
One of the important roles that Air Canada has always played has been in providing leadership in establishing proper safety standards, ensuring that it would give the standard by which others would follow. Similarly, with respect to the question of employee-labour relations, we have been able, through public policy, to establish guidelines and standards for labour relations in the federal sector, which I think have had an important influence on all other sectors. We will lose that capacity.
Even matters such as our language policy, for which we used Air Canada as a carrier of national identity and expression, will no longer have the same ability to influence those decisions. The moment that there is one private share sold under the laws of Canada, Air Canada can no longer be used as an instrument of public policy. It can no longer be our instrument. Rules can be set that Air Canada must abide, like all other private businesses in the federal jurisdiction, but it cannot be
Air Canada
used to demonstrate, to show example, to give a standard. That capacity is lost.
Let me deal with a further question which I think is important. We debate day after day, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, the question of trade in this House. The position of my Party has been that we should be aiming to establish Canada as an international trader and not to confine ourselves to a continental market-place. One of the crucial elements in that strategy is our capacity to establish lines of commerce, exchange and communication with countries around the world.
If we look at the airline industry, we see that it is one of the most important avenues for establishing those commercial connections. One of the reasons why we have such faltering sales in Latin America, for example, is that we have two flights a week to Rio from Canada and that is it. If one wants to travel to the Argentine or to Central America, it is a 15 hour flight from Canada, as opposed to direct flights to those areas which would open up new sales opportunities, as well as new commercial and tourist opportunities. To make that happen, a flag carrier is needed. What is needed is a public airline to establish that type of initiative. That should be a judgment of public policy. We will be dealing with an airline totally dictated by its market-place criteria, its bottom line. It will say: "Look, we can make an awful lot more money by putting our 747s on the London-Toronto run. We do not have time to open up a new line into Rio or Buenos Aires or into Malaysia". Some lines are being opened into Malaysia through negotiation. I think that that could be dictated because it is a Crown corporation and therefore has certain leverage.
What I am saying is that these Bills have been introduced in a total vacuum, in the absence of an airline policy for Canada that would demonstrate what we see as the future role and opportunity for airline travel, both domestically and internationally. There is no sense of what kind of needs we will have, or what our priorities should be, or whether we need a public airline to service those.
If we had done that examination, if we had said that there is the future of our airline industry for Canada in the next 50 years, and then done a proper examination as to what would best service that, what mixture of public or private initiatives, then we could legitimately say whether this Bill serves the purpose or not. It was done without any of that kind of judgment or analysis. So literally, to use an airline analogy, we are flying blind.
We do not know whether we need a public airline or not at this stage because the Government has never bothered to find out from Canadians. It is asking Parliament to pass an important piece of legislation that will take Air Canada out of the public sphere and turn it to the private sphere without knowing whether that is the best judgment in terms of future development for Canada or, in terms of increasing its commitment in high technology, or of ensuring that there is a fair sharing in the regions of Canada, and that we have the ability to protect ourselves abroad.

June 3, 1988
Air Canada
It is legislation that has no roots. It has no context. It has no framework. It is born out of a very basic and very short-term judgment that we do not have $300 million to give Air Canada to buy new airplanes so we will sell it now and get the money so that we can balance our books for the next Budget. That is not the way decisions of this importance should be taken. That is the reason why my Party and I are opposing this particular Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) a few questions. I have a great deal of respect for the Hon. Member. He is a fellow westerner. He has a great deal of experience in politics. He was a former Minister. We have worked together on projects in the past. I want to ask him whether or not he has really changed his mind in terms of privatizing Air Canada.
I happened by fluke to come across a Canadian Press article from May 17, 1984.1 am sure the Conservatives will be happy to know that the headline in the article stated: "Air Canada may be flying into the private sector". The article contained a lengthy interview with a number of people, including the Minister of Transport at the time who is now the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. The lead sentence was: "Has Lloyd Axworthy hung a 'for sale' sign on Air Canada?" The article goes on to state: "Mr. Axworthy's plan to relax regulation of the airline industry has rekindled enthusiasm for putting Air Canada into private hands. Mr. Axworthy will not say whether or not he favours changing ownership of the airline, which has assets of some $2.2 billion". In the article, Mr. Jeanniot, who at that time was the Executive VicePresident of Air Canada, stated: "Mr. Axworthy would not oppose the principle of privatization".
I do not wish to read the whole article since it is fairly lengthy, but certainly in May, 1984, the Canadian Press was convinced that the then Minister of Transport was in favour of the principle of the privatization of Air Canada. It states in the article somewhere that the Minister is willing to have a study done and keep an open mind and see whether or not Air Canada should be sold to the private sector.
I am very happy, of course, that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry is not in favour of privatization of Air Canada. Can he elaborate to the House if indeed he has changed his mind, and why he has done so?

It is unfortunate that the Hon. Member did not listen to my speech. I went through step by step what we did. I pointed out to him that, when we relaxed the rules setting a new airline policy in 1984, it clearly put Air Canada into a new position. I put a reference to the Transport Committee of the House of Commons asking it to examine the role of Air Canada in light of those questions on safety, competition and concentration, labour relations, and regional development. As I pointed out at the time, unfortunately the new Government when it came in in 1984, cancelled that reference.
What I was saying, and I think that I was being open and honest, was that the previous system, which, through unnecessary rules had restricted and limited the routing and pricing for airline policy, had to be relaxed. In light of the U.S. experience with deregulation it was incumbent upon us to determine exactly how we should proceed in Canada. All I did was to make an honest effort to allow Canadians to be heard on a very crucial issue.
Furthermore, I established very clear criteria as to what should be the determination. I was not responding blindly, as some of his colleagues do, against it or for it; I was saying that there are new circumstances that should be examined, Canadians should be heard, we should conduct inquiries, and if it meets some type of criteria then we would act. As I pointed out in my speech, and it is unfortunate that the Member did not listen more carefully, the Government refused to do that. None of the criteria that I have established in terms of a sharing of technology, a sharing of benefits, and a consideration about safety, have been answered. The Government has made no attempt to deal with those issues. There is no airline policy for Canada. Therefore, to privatize Air Canada without having a proper airline policy is a fool's game.

As my hon. colleague travels back and forth to Winnipeg has he noticed any significant change in the service offered, the length of line-ups, the time it takes to check through the baggage, or the time it takes to check through and board the aircraft? Does the Hon. Member think that privatization will add the security that is needed? Is there a withdrawal of the number of staff and people available to service the clientele?
When one listens to some of the airline employees, and I wonder if the Hon. Member has had the same feedback, there have been unconscionable cuts and not necessarily lay-offs, but the gaps have not been filled. As the Hon. Member laid out the parameters of the criteria that should have been examined by a committee of the House, which included not only the regulations but the sharing of benefits, labour relations, competition, and safety, what has the Hon. Member noticed when he has been travelling?

I must confess that this morning I did a quick calculation and discovered that in the last two months I have travelled back and forth to Winnipeg 16 times. With that type of frequency, my only way of coping was to shift my mind into neutral and not even recognize what was going on. That was the only way to deal with that particular vagary. It allows me to lighten up totally and once again become the refreshing and provocative Member of Parliament when I hit the ground in Winnipeg running.
Those types of questions were exactly what I had hoped we would have had a chance to examine. I find it unsettling and disturbing that those are questions that we could have found answers to. We did have the experience of other forms of deregulation or privatizing in other parts of the world that we

June 3, 1988
could have carefully examined. There was no attempt to do that.
This particular legislation is dictated far more by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his imperatives than by the attempt of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to come up with the best mixture of airline policy and the best mixture of airline services for this country. We are doing it for the wrong reasons.
Unless I see someone else, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) can have the floor for the second time.

When the Hon. Member for Cowichan- Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) rose, I stated that I thought the Conservative Party had made a very abrupt change from a historical position on public ownership in our country. It was the Party across the way that brought in things like the Wheat Board, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the CNR, and other agencies of that type. Now it seems to be following the policy of Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher when it comes to planning our economy and our society. I suggest that some long-time members of the Conservative Party, for example, the Chairman of the Transport Committee, are probably extremely upset with this abrupt change in direction in a vision for our country.
Can the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry shed some light on why the Conservative Party has made this very abrupt change? There must be some reason for it, other than blind devotion to the ideology of Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, which is importing an ideology from another country. Can the Hon. Member shed some light as to why the Conservative Party is doing this and changing the country that we have all fought so hard to build?

For the life of me, I have never been able to figure out why anyone is a Conservative anyway, so to try to figure out why someone thinks like one is certainly beyond my capacity. I think that would require a whole assembly of Freudian psychologists to work that particular problem out.
I should point out to the Hon. Member that it is important to remember that in the United States the deregulation policy was initiated by President Jimmy Carter. In fact, it was Senator Ted Kennedy, who was known as one of the strong left-wing Liberals in the United States' political spectrum, who initiated that through his studies in the United States Senate.
To return to my point, I do not think that we should be debating on ideological terms. The real success in Canada has been to determine how we use public Crown corporations in a pragmatic, utilitarian way. Our judgment has been: "If you need a Crown corporation, then do it." If there is a public role, a public service, and a public reason for doing it, then have a Crown corporation. If those reasons come to an end, then get rid of it. The problem is that this Bill is not using that judgment. There is no basis for making that judgment in anything the Minister of Transport or his colleagues have
Air Canada
stated. I think it was dictated frankly and purely out of the fact that the Government does not want to spend $300 million to refinance an Air Canada fleet. That is the reason the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) changed his mind. I think that the Minister of Finance simply said: "We can't afford $300 million, so sell the airline". It is as simple as that.
That is not a reason to sell one of the most valuable and important public assets in this country. Perhaps in a few years we will need a public Air Canada.
On debate, the Hon. Minister of State for Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis).

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I just want to point out that government Members were prepared to stay a little later today to finish this important business, and to advise the House that the business on Monday will be Bill C-129.
The Minister will know that that is hardly a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I want to point out that if the Minister and the Conservative Government would get their act together he would not have to make a point of order that is not a point of order.
That is also not a point of order. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, before the Conservatives flee from the House, I want to remind them of the promise that was made by the Leader of the Conservative Party on January 15, 1985. He gave assurances that the federal Government had no plans to sell either the CBC or Air Canada.
Now that the Government has flip-flopped on this one, I presume the next thing we will see is its decision to put CBC on the block as well. It is shameful that a government that was elected on a platform that Canadians needed a government that people could trust and that it was a Party bent on kicking out the Liberal Government to bring in something more positive has turned around and given the country exactly the opposite.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) says that something is a sacred trust, we know that means the opposite. When the Prime Minister says that Air Canada is not for sale, we know now that it is not true. Whatever he says today is liable to be turned around tomorrow.
One of the basic issues in the forthcoming election campaign will be exactly that question: Can you trust the man who has been Prime Minister for the last four years? Is he to be trusted if he says in the next election that he will do something for battered wives or child benefits? You cannot trust him on Air Canada.
One of the first things his Government did after it took power in 1984 was to deindex the income tax system. Then it tried to deindex the old age pensions after the Prime Minister said that pensions and help for pensioners was a sacred trust. This gang cannot shoot straight and this gang cannot be trusted.
I am raising this because I think the Government itself has to realize just how profound is the deception, disaffection and disillusionment among Canadians since the Conservatives came to power in 1984.
There has been some improvement in terms of economic performance of our country. That has happened because of international factors and because of a spillover of economic growth from the United States. That probably would have happened under any Party in power. However, it has not affected how people perceive the Conservatives. There is some justice to their perception because people understand that whether or not there are more jobs or some improvement in certain areas of the economy, a lot more than that is needed. We need integrity in this country, we need honesty, and we have not been getting that. Instead, there has been a succession of scandals, an unprecedented succession of Ministers having to leave office under a cloud or facing various charges in the court and so on.
The public has had to shell out for expensive inquiries around members of the Cabinet. It is no wonder this has come right back into the hands of the man who leads the country, the Prime Minister.
When the Government announced in April that it intended to privatize Air Canada, it is no wonder that people responded by saying it was a betrayal. That is exactly what it is.

Mr. Speaker, personally, I have considerable doubts about the integrity and honesty of this Government, and I remember a meeting the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had with Mr. Laberge of the QFL, the first in a series of consultations with leaders of the labour movement in Canada, on January 15, 1985. When the Prime Minister met reporters upon leaving the meeting, he said: "Some people want to buy the CBC. The CBC is not for sale! Air Canada is not for sale!" Mr. Speaker, how can we trust a Prime Minister who makes statements that are completely turned around in a matter of days or months?

Recently there was another example of that exact question about the credibility of the Government and the kind of tawdry, sleazy government it is intent on giving to Canada. That example was the announcement made a few days ago that the Government intends to spend some $30 million of taxpayer's money on an advertising PR campaign for the free trade agreement. Some of that money has already been spent.
The Minister responsible for the trade agreement has hired the campaign manager who ran his leadership campaign in 1984 to direct this particular effort. The Minister is now jetting across Canada, going to barbecues and attending meetings, to say that free trade is good.
Until now, the campaigns have not affected the public's perception much, and people continue to say that they have grave misgivings about the trade agreement. They have even greater misgivings about that kind of misuse of public funds. They ask how the Conservatives can cough up a billion dollars to bail out some western banks, including some $300 million to foreign banks who had short-term deposits in western banks. These are not ranchers or farmers, these are not senior citizens
June 3, 1988

eking out their living in retirement on the basis of money they deposited with the Canadian Commercial Bank or Northland Bank. These are big money machines in the United States and abroad that happened to put money in short-term deposits in these two banks in Canada, knowing the risk. They were compensated.
If Air Canada needs $300 million for equipment, why could that money not have been put aside? Instead, the Government could have put $700 million into Northland and CCB and kept the remaining money to ensure that Air Canada would not be sold by a Government that claims it is starved for money.
The same Government that says it must sell Air Canada is capable of turning around and saying the defence of the Arctic in this country requires Canada to have a dozen nuclear-powered submarines at a cost it says is $8 billion but which every expert says will approach $16 billion.
I think you should ask the average Canadian, Mr. Speaker, whether on balance people would prefer that we have an extra submarine or that we put half or one-third of the money the sub would cost into keeping Air Canada as a national instrument and as a company that continues to be owned by all Canadians.
One thing that puzzles me about this-
It doesn't take much to puzzle you.

-is how the devil can you sell to Canadians something that Canadians already own? I really wonder about that. We are not talking about broadening the ownership of Air Canada, we are talking about narrowing it.
After privatization takes place, if it does take place, then we will see a few thousand Canadians, some Americans or other foreigners who will control Air Canada whether or not their shareholding is 45 per cent or 100 per cent. There, too, we have an example of deception of the Government and dishonesty of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister responsible, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) and others for this particular move. That dishonesty lies in the fact that the Government is trying to maintain that the majority stake in Air Canada is kept in the hands of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard). But the Minister of Transport and the Minister responsible for this deal, the Deputy Prime Minister, have specifically announced that 55 per cent ownership will be a passive ownership and will not be voted. In other words, it will follow decisions made by the directors who were selected by the private sector shareholders. That it seems to me does not leave us in a very good position at all. It means that Air Canada's control will have effectively been sold, whether or not the majority of the shares remain in the hands of the Minister of Transport.
May I say, as the spokesperson for finance for my Party- and I want to be quite specific-that if we arrive in government in a few months' time, and there is very much a prospect
Air Canada
of that happening, and we find that 55 per cent of the shares in Air Canada continue to be in the hands of the Minister of Transport, we will not feel bound by promises made by the Government now that that will be a passive holding which will go exactly the way the private shareholders want it to go. That is an unconscionable commitment, a commitment which no government should make. If the people of Canada own the majority of Air Canada, then they should have the right to direct Air Canada just as it is done in the private sector.
Suggestions from the private sector that because Air Canada is publicly owned it somehow acts unfairly are just plain bunkum. The Chairman of Air Canada, who favours privatization, regrettably, has strongly reacted to any suggestion that Air Canada is operating under unfair business practices. Mr. Taylor responded to a critique by CP Air saying, "It is not our size that bothers the President of CP Air, it is our skill". He added, "Our shareholding community is 25 million Canadian citizens, and a great many of them feel a direct interest in our company". I think that is important. I will come to this question in just a second about what I believe is genuinely public enterprise culture which has served this country extremely well. It would be tragic to back away from it in the case of Air Canada. When Canadians see the Maple Leaf in the circle which is the Air Canada logo, they know it is theirs.
I can remember the day 10 or 15 years ago when perhaps Air Canada had too great a market share, too much control over the markets and it was criticized. The service was not as good as it might have been. Let me point out how the service in Air Canada has improved. This airline has won efficiency, tourists, courtesy, service and safety awards consistently over the years. Its operating statistics have put it in the upper rank of airlines in North America. Air Canada is a good airline.
I want to say to Mr. Taylor and Mr. Jeanniot and all the men and women who are employees of Air Canada that as one Canadian I am proud of Air Canada. I do not think we should try to punish them by selling it off and saying we are ashamed of the contribution it has made to this country over the course of the last few years.
I would say as well that if the Government had evidence that Air Canada was overstaffed and had evidence that it was being run inefficiently, the Government has had three and a half years to use its control of Air Canada to change it. The Government could and have replaced the Chairman or President of Air Canada and brought in new management and told them to do a decent job.
At British Air about one-third of the workforce was cut before Margaret Thatcher sold the company into the private sector. There were some real staff problems, but those problems do not exist with Air Canada or, if they do, I certainly have not heard them discussed by the Government as part of its justification for the sale.
What does the Government try to maintain? It maintains that Air Canada will become an unprofitable airline unless it is

June 3, 1988
Air Canada
privatized. Over the last 10 years Air Canada has made profits of over $300 million. It has had profits in 10 of the last 12 years. There is absolutely no evidence that that will change. In fact, last year Air Canada's profits would have been upwards of $100 million if it had not been for a labour dispute toward the end of the year.
The Government says that unless Air Canada is privatized it will not able to replace its fleet of aircraft over the next few years because it will not be able to raise the capital to finance the move. I am not exactly sure what analogy to give to this, but let us consider the example of parents providing room and board for their son or daughter so that he or she can go to university and then turning around and saying to that son or daughter, "You have to pay for the room and board", to which the son or daughter replies, "Then I can't go to university". Parents will then blame their child for dropping out of university because he or she refuses to pay the room and board because it was not being provided by the parent in a parental role.
If I can come back to the corporate matter we, the people of Canada, own Air Canada. We own the equity of Air Canada. Air Canada has not had any equity from its owners over the last 10 years despite enormous changes in aviation internationally and nationally over the course of that period of time. Air Canada has done an outstanding job of maintaining competitiveness, of changing the way it operates, of providing competitive fares so people can fly across this country from time to time and return for $300 or $400, bringing air travel within the reach of many people who could not afford fares the way they were eight or ten years ago.
The reason that Air Canada cannot reasonably get those new aircraft is the Government refuses. The Government says it will not give it any equity, but then says Air Canada cannot compete to get new aircraft because it has no equity. Of course it has no equity because the Government will not give Air Canada any equity.
We know there was a shoot-out on this issue between the then Minister of Transport, who is now the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Air Canada came along and said it needed $300 million in equity. The Government said no, and the Minister responsible, the Deputy Prime Minister, then went ahead with privatization. The Government created a crisis where no crisis needed to exist.
The Government, which cannot find $300 million equity, has not explored other means such as lease-backs, nor has there been any published statement about the kinds of concessional terms available from aircraft manufacturers to assist with the financing of the new fleet that Air Canada needs over the course of the next 15 years. The airline needs to spend a couple of billion dollars. It is a lot of money and some of the money has to be in the form of equity. As a New Democrat I understand and accept that. If my Party were in power, the Minister of Finance of my Party would ensure that
the equity which Air Canada needs, if that is the solution, can and would be found within the budget of the people of Canada in order to allow Air Canada to remain as a national and publicly owned airline.
Let us come back to the question that if the Government can spend $16 billion or $18 billion on a number of submarines, what is wrong with keeping Air Canada in public hands? If the Government can spend close to $1 billion on a low-level air defence system which, believe it or not, will protect two military airports in West Germany as part of our NATO commitment, then why can it not come up with $300 million for Air Canada?
I do not believe that the entire $300 million is needed today. I have had a look at Air Canada's balance sheet. It needs some infusion of equity, but if it were assured that it could have $100 million as of July 1 and a further injection of capital in, let's say, April of next year, and the rest in March or April of 1990, that would do the job. That would ensure that Air Canada could go forward confidently and order the new aircraft it needs. That would avoid the loss of control of this airline as a consequence of the Government's short-sighted policies.
Then they say that the federal Government has overextended itself in support of Air Canada. I am not sure what they are talking about. There have not been public funds going into Air Canada. This has not been like de Havilland or Canadair. Then they say that Air Canada will become leaner, meaner and more efficient if it goes into private hands. That case has not been proved. The Chairman of Air Canada himself says that it is an efficient airline.
The Chairman and the President of Air Canada say that Canadian consumers would immediately see the benefits of a privatized Air Canada in lower fares and aggressive fights for passengers. If I were the Minister of Transport, I would call those folk in and say: "What the devil are you doing? You say you can cut fares if we follow your campaign to become privatized". That is blackmail on the part of Mr. Jeanniot and Mr. Taylor. It is nothing less.
As the Chairman and the President of Air Canada responsible for a Crown corporation, they have been acting quite improperly and inappropriately in the launching of the privatization campaign that they have launched consistently over the last several years. I believe that if the Government had any gumption at all, it would tell the Chairman and the President: "You are our airline right now. We speak for the people of Canada. You quit that campaign for privatization. That is a decision that we as a Government will take. Don't try to force our hands".
I would like to conclude with some notes that go back to that great Canadian, Sir John A. Macdonald. As my friend, Herschel Hardin, in his excellent book A Nation Unaware: The Canadian Economic Culture, pointed out several years
June 3, 1988

ago, this country has had and has now a public enterprise culture. We have good and efficient railways because we have Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. Canadian National was the result of lousy investments in the private sector initially, but it has given Canada very efficient rail service. There is the CBC and private television broadcasting in healthy competition. The public sector helps to set the standards and to ensure service to all Canadians across this broad and diverse country. I know that in the event that the broadcasting sector really falls down on the job, the CBC will be there to do it.
We have Petro-Canada and private oil companies. We have private and public companies in other sectors as well. While it may seem that there is reasonable competition between Canadian Airlines International, Wardair and Air Canada right now, we do not have the assurance that that will continue. It could simply collapse the way the U.S. airline industry almost collapsed after deregulation under Reagan just a few years ago. We could have chaos and we would have no national instrument.
Just because the Government feels that the instrument of national policy in air transportation may not be needed today-and I do not agree with the Government-that is no reason to abandon it and do away with a national instrument for public policy in the passenger and freight aviation sectors should it be needed in the year 1995 or the year 2005. For all of those reasons, I believe that this country can afford to keep Air Canada in public hands. It should be able to afford to keep Air Canada as an instrument of public policy and it should be proud of the job Air Canada has done over the last half century.

Mr. Speaker, as the finance critic for the New Democratic Party, I am sure my hon. colleague is aware of the very heavy tax burdens that have been placed on the Canadian people over the last four years by the Conservative Government. There is a lot of concern on the part of the Government about the deficit.
Does my colleague see the sale of Air Canada as being one possible way of reducing the deficit? If so, how significant an impact would it have on reducing the deficit? Would that in any way result in lower taxes for the hard-pressed Canadian taxpayers?

Mr. Speaker, the effect on the deficit of this particular measure would be minuscule. It would be infinitesimal. It would be absolutely microscopic. It would be insignificant. It would be invisible. It could not be seen in any meaningful way. I do hope I make myself clear.
Let us look at the figures. The national debt of Canada currently runs somewhere over $250 billion, and that is uncomfortably high. Our annual deficit is running at something like $28 billion or $29 billion a year. I am not sure how the Government would deal with the money received from the sale of shares in Air Canada. Does it really want to sell the
Air Canada
jewels and use that money to pay for the groceries? That is essentially what would happen if all of that $300 million were to be put against the deficit. If it were put against the deficit, it would represent 1 per cent of one year's deficit. That would be the total reduction.
If the Government really wants to reduce the deficit, let it cut back on spending programs for nuclear submarines. I think Canadians would be an awful lot happier about owning an airline which encourages international co-operation than they would about having a dozen nuclear subs which would be increasing confrontation between the western powers and the powers in the Soviet bloc.
If the Government were to invest that money, it would return about $30 million a year. That would be meaningful in the sense that it would reduce the annual deficit of Canada, at its current rate, by about one-tenth of 1 per cent on a continuing basis. That is a very small sum indeed.
Finally, I have been reading in some commentaries in the financial press the suggestion that the benefit of the sale of the shares will provide the $300 million in equity that Air Canada needs. If I understand that correctly, that means that the Treasury will not get a dime in order to reduce the deficit. Air Canada is not costing us any money right now. There is no annual pay-out to Air Canada the way there is to VIA Rail. This move would simply provide Air Canada with $300 million in equity, and there has been no rationale or serious attempt to look for various other ways to find that money. The only argument then is that if we were to proceed and to provide that equity, there would be some charge which would either have to be met by lower expenses elsewhere, such as on nuclear subs, or else by an increase in the deficit. However, it is not worth half a bag of chicken feed relative to the over-all size of the deficit of the Government of Canada.
